A screenshot carries the same data as text, and mobile numbers and emails still identify people once the names are gone.

quiz.prompt: A colleague forwards you a customer's complaint letter (full name, home address and account number included) and asks you to use AI to rewrite the reply more politely. What should you do?

options.text: Paste it as it is: your colleague collected the data, so the duty of care for it sits with them.
Swap the name, address and account number for placeholders, paste the rest, and fill the details back in after.
Use it as it stands but delete the chat afterwards, so the customer's details are not left in your history.
Rewrite the reply by hand from scratch instead, since a customer complaint is never something AI should be anywhere near.

quiz.explanation: The Data Privacy Act gives people rights over information that describes them and puts duties on the organisations holding it, so passing a customer's details to a third-party AI company is a disclosure nobody agreed to. Deleting the chat afterwards does not undo it, and placeholders get you the same rewrite without sending anything identifying.

quiz.prompt: Your employer has no written policy about AI tools and nobody has ever mentioned them. You want to use a chatbot to draft internal reports. What is the sensible move?

options.text: Read the absence of a policy as permission, and stop if someone later says the company would rather you did not.
Use a paid personal plan rather than the free one, since paid plans come with stronger data terms for work.
Assume it is not allowed and leave the question alone, since raising it invites a no you cannot take back.
Ask your manager in writing, say what you would and would not paste, and keep the reply you get back.

quiz.explanation: Silence is not permission, and never asking leaves you exposed either way. A written answer you have kept protects you if it is questioned later, and naming what you would and would not paste makes it easy for a manager to say yes, or to say yes on the company account.

quiz.prompt: You are writing the AI line on your CV. Which one holds up best when an interviewer says "walk me through that"?

options.text: "Proficient with ChatGPT, Claude and Google Sheets; comfortable writing prompts for drafting, summarising and formatting work."
"Use AI daily to draft product copy, cutting turnaround time sharply and freeing hours for higher-value work."
"Draft weekly Shopee listings from a spec sheet in ChatGPT, checking every price and dimension against the supplier file."
"Experienced in AI-assisted content production, with strong attention to accuracy and a careful review process on every draft."

quiz.explanation: The credible unit is a workflow: the repeated task, the tool, what you prepare, and the specific check you run. A tool list, an improvement claim with no measurement behind it, and adjectives about your own accuracy all invite a follow-up question you cannot answer.

quiz.prompt: On a discovery call a prospective client says: "Why would I pay you when ChatGPT can write these for free?" Which response follows what this lesson recommends?

options.text: Name the parts that are yours (the spec sheet, the style rules, the check) and what goes wrong without them.
Point out that AI-written copy comes out generic and inaccurate, and that their customers will be able to tell straight away.
Agree that the tools have changed, and offer a lower rate on this project so that you stay competitive on price.
Explain that you do not use AI on client work at all, so what they are buying is entirely written by hand.

quiz.explanation: Arguing that AI does not work is not credible to someone who has seen it work, and dropping your rate concedes the point. Moving the conversation to the material you prepare, the checks you run and who is accountable for an error puts it on ground the model cannot cover.

assignment.title: The One-Task AI Workflow
assignment.brief_mdx:
Pick one task you genuinely repeat (a weekly report, a batch of customer replies, class notes, product listings, a posting schedule) and submit a single text document with six short parts.

1. **The task.** What it is, the steps you do now, and roughly how long it takes each time.
2. **The workflow.** The same task rewritten as ordered steps, each marked AI or you, with one sentence on why the human steps stay human.
3. **The standing prompt.** The full prompt you would paste every time, covering context, task, constraints and output format, written so a co-worker could run it unchanged.
4. **One real run.** The output you actually got, pasted in. Trim it to about 300 words if it is long.
5. **Your check.** What you verified and against which source outside the AI, including at least one thing the model got wrong or that you could not confirm.
6. **Two honest sentences.** How you would describe this skill to an employer or client.

Everything is submitted as text, with no file uploads. Before you submit, remove or replace real names, client details and personal data. Doing that properly is part of what is being marked.
criteria: The task is genuinely repeating, with the current steps and a rough time given, not a one-off and not a vague 'write content'
The workflow separates AI steps from human steps, and the human steps sit where a mistake would actually cost something
The standing prompt contains context, task, constraints and output format, and is complete enough for someone else to paste and run unchanged
The verification section names specific items checked against a real source outside the AI, and reports at least one error or unconfirmed claim
Real names, client details and personal data have been removed or replaced, with a sign that the learner understands why
The closing description matches what was actually built: no 'AI expert', no invented results or figures
